edges.description: Reproduces placental viral persistence with inflammation and haemorrhage, fetal infection, and dose-dependent fetal injury and loss after primary maternal infection in early pregnancy.
edges.limitations: Mouse placentation differs from human placentation, infection is by intravaginal inoculation of a set viral dose at gestation day 4.5, and the model addresses the intrauterine route only, not the intrapartum route that accounts for most human cases.

nodes.description: Structural brain abnormality is reported in intrauterine infection, where the insult falls during fetal brain development rather than after birth.

nodes.description: Marked transaminase elevation reflects hepatic involvement in disseminated disease, and at ten times the upper limit of normal at the start of therapy it is associated with mortality.

evidence.reference_title: Natural history of neonatal herpes simplex virus infections in the acyclovir era.
evidence.snippet: Among patients with disseminated HSV disease treated with acyclovir at 30 mg/kg/d, mortality was associated with aspartate transaminase elevations of >/=10 times the upper limit of normal at the time of initiation of acyclovir therapy.

nodes.description: Fever with convulsions in the first weeks of life is the presentation that should raise suspicion, particularly when empirical antibacterial treatment fails.

nodes.description: Bloodborne spread to multiple organs produces the disseminated form, the presentation with the highest mortality. Which of the three forms develops is the principal determinant of outcome and sets the duration of aciclovir therapy.

nodes.description: Pregnant mice infected intravaginally with HSV-2 on gestation day 4.5. Viral DNA persists in placental tissue, with placental inflammation and haemorrhage, transmission to fetal tissue, and dose-dependent reduction in fetal and placental weight and fetal loss.
nodes.id: Intravaginal primary HSV-2 infection in early-pregnant C57BL/6 mice

evidence.reference_title: Primary HSV-2 Infection in Early Pregnancy Results in Transplacental Viral Transmission and Dose-Dependent Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes in a Novel Mouse Model.
evidence.snippet: This mouse model shows a dose-dependent effect of primary HSV-2 infection on pregnancy outcomes and suggests that fetal loss may occur due to placental inflammation, thus providing valuable insight into in utero transmission of HSV-2.

nodes.description: Intravenous aciclovir is the treatment, with intensity and duration tailored to which of the three presentations is present. Availability of safe, effective antiviral therapy together with PCR diagnosis is described as having transformed management of this disease.

evidence.reference_title: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection: From the maternal infection to the child outcome.
evidence.snippet: the treatment with acyclovir should be tailored according to symptoms and signs of infection, and virological tests

nodes.description: After intrapartum acquisition the virus replicates at the site of inoculation - skin, eye or oropharyngeal mucosa. Disease that stays here is the skin, eye and mouth (SEM) form, the least severe of the three presentations.
nodes.id: Local Mucocutaneous Replication at the Portal of Entry

evidence.reference_title: Congenital herpes simplex with ophthalmic and multisystem features: a case report.
evidence.snippet: Neonatal HSV can manifest with isolated mucocutaneous lesions, neurological involvement, or disseminated disease.

nodes.description: The reservoir. Maternal infection is categorised as primary first episode, non-primary first episode, or recurrent, and primary maternal infection is a recognised risk factor for transmission, alongside vaginal delivery and prolonged rupture of membranes. Shedding is frequently asymptomatic, so the exposure can occur without any maternal history.

evidence.reference_title: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection: From the maternal infection to the child outcome.
evidence.snippet: We summarized the three clinical categories of maternal HSV infection during pregnancy (primary first episode, nonprimary first episode, or recurrent episode) and the mechanisms of fetal damage.

evidence.reference_title: Congenital herpes simplex with ophthalmic and multisystem features: a case report.
evidence.snippet: risk factors for mother-to-child transmission include vaginal delivery, primary maternal infection, and prolonged rupture of membranes.

nodes.description: Antiviral prophylaxis given to the mother in late pregnancy reduces genital HSV recurrence and viral shedding at delivery, which is the exposure that transmits the infection. Whether it reduces neonatal herpes itself is not established - the disease is rare enough that the trials are underpowered for that endpoint. Recorded here because prevention is the principal clinical lever in this disease.

evidence.reference_title: Third trimester antiviral prophylaxis for preventing maternal genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) recurrences and neonatal infection.
evidence.snippet: Women who received antiviral prophylaxis were significantly less likely to have a recurrence of genital herpes at delivery (relative risk (RR) 0.28, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.18 to 0.43

evidence.reference_title: Third trimester antiviral prophylaxis for preventing maternal genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) recurrences and neonatal infection.
evidence.snippet: There is insufficient evidence to determine if antiviral prophylaxis reduces the incidence of neonatal herpes.

nodes.description: Spread to the central nervous system produces the CNS form, which may present with overt neurological signs or with nonspecific illness. This is one of the two severe presentations and the one that carries neurodevelopmental sequelae.

evidence.reference_title: The Many Faces of Neurological Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus Infection.
evidence.snippet: The wide range of clinical presentations of CNS manifestations in neonatal HSV infection, ranging from nonspecific to evident neurological symptoms, underscores the need for a high index of suspicion

nodes.description: Ocular involvement is a presenting feature that can lead to the diagnosis. Reported manifestations include blepharoconjunctivitis, keratitis and panuveitis, and ocular assessment has been argued to be decisive in the diagnostic workup.

evidence.reference_title: Congenital herpes simplex with ophthalmic and multisystem features: a case report.
evidence.snippet: Later, a new ocular examination was suggestive of panuveitis.

nodes.description: On the intrauterine route, viral persistence in placental tissue produces inflammation and haemorrhage, reduced placental and fetal weight, and fetal loss at higher viral doses. This is the step that distinguishes congenital from perinatal disease, and it is why the intrauterine form presents with malformation rather than with postnatal illness.

nodes.description: Virus reaches the infant by one of three routes, dominated by intrapartum contact. Which route operates determines the presentation: in utero transmission damages the developing fetus, intrapartum transmission produces neonatal disease after a latent interval.
nodes.id: Vertical Transmission to Fetus or Neonate

evidence.reference_title: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection: From the maternal infection to the child outcome.
evidence.snippet: Considering when the transmission of the infection from the mother to the fetus/newborn occurs, three types of neonatal infection can be distinguished: intrauterine infection (5% of cases), postnatal infection (10% of cases), and perinatal infections (85% of cases).

nodes.description: Grouped vesicles of skin, and lesions of eye and mouth, define the localised presentation. They are not a reliable sign of the disease as a whole: a large minority of infants never have skin vesicles at presentation or during the acute illness, and that proportion is highest in disseminated disease.

evidence.reference_title: Intrauterine Herpes Simplex Virus Infection: Insights Into a Silent Threat.
evidence.snippet: On the fourth day of life, grouped vesicles emerged, leading to the initiation of intravenous acyclovir therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Natural history of neonatal herpes simplex virus infections in the acyclovir era.
evidence.snippet: A significant minority of patients did not have skin vesicles at the time of their presentation and did not develop them during the acute HSV disease (39% of patients with disseminated disease; 32% of patients with central nervous system [CNS] disease; and 17% of patients with skin, eye, and/or mouth disease).
